title: Bulk Production Planning
subtitle: Plan, cost, staff and deliver a large order on time, with quality checked all the way through and the cash to carry it.
description: Learn to turn a big enquiry into a written specification, measure your true capacity, calculate every material, and build a backward schedule with quality gates. You will cost the full run, close the cash gap with sound payment terms, staff the line safely and finish with a bulk readiness portfolio, following one worked order of 5,000 packs from enquiry to delivery.
outcomes: Turn a bulk enquiry into a one-page order specification sheet agreed with the buyer
Calculate your bottleneck, sustained daily rate and takt time, and state your realistic capacity
Build a material requirements sheet and a backward production schedule with milestones and buffer days
Design quality gates with sampling, a stop rule and a quality log for a long run
Cost a full run, find the cash gap and negotiate payment terms that fund production
Staff and lead the run safely, deliver with signed proof and review results for the next order
audience: Women producers in food, crafts, fashion or household products who already sell regularly and want to accept large orders from companies, schools, events or distributors with confidence.
tools: Smartphone with a stopwatch, calculator and camera
Notebook or Google Sheets for trackers, costing and cash plans
Digital scale and a known test weight (for products sold by weight)
Calendar for working days and holidays
WhatsApp Business for buyer, supplier and team communication
Your own production records for at least 10 working days

modules.title: Sizing the Order: Specification, Capacity and Materials
modules.overview: Before you say yes to a big order, you need three sets of numbers: exactly what the buyer wants, how many units your workshop can truly make per day, and how much material the full run will eat. This module builds all three, using one running example: 5,000 packs of plantain chips for a company's end-of-year hampers.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a bulk order: the order specification sheet and what changes with size
objectives: List the eight facts every bulk order must state before work starts
Write a one-page order specification sheet from a buyer's WhatsApp message
Calculate how materials, labour hours, storage and cash grow with order size
Spot the gaps in a bulk enquiry and ask the right questions

blocks.text: A bulk order is not your normal work made bigger. When an order is 50 or 100 times your usual size, five things change at once: the **materials** you must buy before you earn anything, the **labour hours** at your slowest step, the **space** to store raw materials and finished goods, the **cash** you must spend before the buyer pays, and the **risk** that one mistake is copied into thousands of units. Planning means turning each of these into numbers before you agree to a price or a date.

blocks.name: factory
blocks.alt: People working at a production line in a small factory
blocks.caption: A bulk order turns your kitchen or workshop into a small production line, so you plan it like one.

blocks.text: Start with a written specification

Most bulk enquiries in Nigeria arrive as a phone call or a WhatsApp voice note: "We need about 5,000 packs of chips before Christmas, what is your price?" That message is missing almost everything you need. Your first job is to turn it into an **order specification sheet**: one page that you and the buyer both agree on, and that every later plan in this course refers back to.

items: **Product and specification:** exact product, size or weight per unit (for example 100 g), recipe or material, colour, flavour, finish.
**Quantity:** the exact number, and whether the buyer accepts a small plus or minus (for example 5,000 packs, no shortfall accepted).
**Packaging and labelling:** pouch type, the buyer's logo or yours, units per carton, carton markings, any batch code or best-before date.
**Quality standard:** the approved sample both sides keep, and what counts as a defect.
**Delivery:** date, time window, address, who receives, whether one delivery or several.
**Price and payment terms:** unit price, deposit, when the balance is paid and how (bank transfer, Paystack link, Moniepoint).
**Documents:** invoice, delivery note, any regulatory numbers the buyer requires (for packaged food, ask whether they require a NAFDAC registration number).
**Contact and changes:** one named person on each side, and the rule that any change is confirmed in writing.

blocks.title: Ask for the approved sample early
blocks.text: Send three sample units, have the buyer approve one in writing, and keep an identical twin in a sealed, labelled bag at your workshop. This is your golden sample. Every quality check in the run compares against it, and it settles arguments at delivery.
Scaling: what grows, and how fast

Materials grow in a straight line with quantity: 125 times the packs means 125 times the plantain. But some things grow faster than you expect. Storage becomes a real problem, because 5,000 packs fill about 100 cartons. Waste that you ignore in a small batch becomes thousands of naira. And the time at your slowest step, called the **bottleneck**, decides your finishing date, not the hours of your fastest worker.

blocks.title: Worked example: from 40 packs to 5,000 packs
blocks.context: For example, Kemi makes plantain chips in Ibadan. A normal weekend order is 40 packs of 100 g. A company's HR officer asks for 5,000 packs for staff hampers. Her own records show she uses about 0.30 kg of raw plantain and 0.025 litres of frying oil per pack, her fryer produces about 80 packs an hour, and 50 packs fill one carton.
steps: Size ratio: 5,000 divided by 40 = 125 times her normal order.
Raw plantain: 40 packs need 40 x 0.30 = 12 kg. 5,000 packs need 5,000 x 0.30 = 1,500 kg, about one and a half tonnes, before any waste allowance.
Frying oil: 40 x 0.025 = 1 litre, against 5,000 x 0.025 = 125 litres.
Fryer time: 40 packs take 40 / 80 = 0.5 hours. 5,000 packs take 5,000 / 80 = 62.5 hours of frying alone.
Storage: 5,000 / 50 = 100 cartons to keep clean, dry and off the floor until delivery.
blocks.result: The order is not "a busy weekend". It is 62.5 hours of frying, 1.5 tonnes of plantain and 100 cartons of storage. Kemi now knows she must plan days, not hours, and that she needs a clean storage corner before the first carton is sealed.

blocks.title: Small order versus bulk order
items: Small order (40 packs)
Bulk order (5,000 packs)
blocks.caption: The same product needs a different way of working once the order is many times your normal size.

blocks.text: Questions to send back to the buyer

Reply to the enquiry with questions, not a price. A short WhatsApp message works: thank them, then ask for the exact quantity, the delivery date and address, the packaging they expect, whether they need their branding on the pouch, and their usual payment terms. Say you will send a written quotation and a sample within a stated number of days. Serious buyers respect this, and it protects you from quoting for the wrong job.

blocks.title: Watch for fake bulk orders
blocks.text: Be careful with a "bulk order" that asks you to pay a registration fee, buy materials from a supplier they name, or that sends more money than the invoice and asks for a refund of the difference. Confirm the company exists, speak to a named person on an office line, and never release goods or refunds until payment has actually landed in your account, not just a screenshot or SMS alert.
Once both sides sign or confirm the specification sheet, save it as a PDF and pin it in your WhatsApp chat with the buyer. Every later step, from capacity to delivery, uses its numbers.

takeaways: A bulk order changes materials, labour, storage, cash and risk all at once.
Turn every enquiry into a one-page order specification sheet before quoting.
Keep a buyer-approved golden sample at your workshop.
Time at your slowest step, the bottleneck, decides how long the order takes.
Confirm payments in your account, never from screenshots or SMS alerts.

activity.title: Write your order specification sheet
steps: Pick a product you make and imagine an order 100 times your usual size, or use a real enquiry.
Fill in the eight sections of the specification sheet on paper or in a phone note.
Calculate materials, bottleneck hours and cartons for the full quantity, as Kemi did.
Write the WhatsApp reply with your questions to the buyer.
activity.evidence: A photo of your completed one-page specification sheet and your scaling calculation.

lessons.title: Measuring true capacity: the bottleneck, your sustained daily rate and takt time
objectives: Time each step of your process and find the bottleneck
Work out a sustained daily rate from your own production records
Calculate takt time and the daily output an order requires
Decide whether an order fits your capacity, with a clear gap figure

blocks.text: **Capacity** is the number of good units your workshop can make in a day, day after day, without quality falling. Many producers quote from their best-ever day. That is a trap: long runs bring tired hands, material delays, power cuts and cleaning time. This lesson gives you three numbers to replace guesswork: your **bottleneck rate**, your **sustained daily rate** and the order's **takt time**.

blocks.name: stopwatch
blocks.caption: Timing each step with your phone's stopwatch is the start of honest capacity planning.

blocks.text: Step 1: time every step and find the bottleneck

List the steps of your process in order. Then, on a normal day, use your phone's stopwatch to time how many units each step finishes in one hour with the people normally assigned to it. Time each step at least three times and use the average. The step with the lowest rate per hour is the **bottleneck**. The whole line can never go faster than that step, however hard everyone else works.
Here frying, at 80 packs an hour, is the bottleneck. Sealing at 90 is close behind, which matters later: if Kemi speeds up frying, sealing becomes the new bottleneck.

blocks.title: The line moves at the bottleneck's pace
items: Peel and slice: 120/hr
Fry: 80/hr (bottleneck)
Season: 150/hr
Fill and seal: 90/hr
Label and carton: 200/hr
blocks.caption: Every step after the fryer can only work on what the fryer releases, so 80 packs an hour sets the pace.

blocks.text: Step 2: from best day to sustained rate

Kemi's shift is 8 hours. She spends about 1 hour on setting up, heating oil, cleaning and breaks, so the fryer runs about 7 hours. Her **theoretical best day** is 80 x 7 = 560 packs. Real days are lower. Take your own records of finished, good units for your last 10 full working days and calculate the average. If you have no records, run a trial week and count. The average is your **sustained daily rate**. The lowest day tells you how bad a normal bad day gets.

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi's sustained rate and takt time
blocks.context: For example, Kemi's notebook shows good packs for her last 10 full days: 520, 470, 455, 500, 430, 480, 460, 440, 470 and 475. The order is 5,000 packs, and she plans to make 2% extra for quality samples and rejects, so 5,100 packs. Her fryer runs 7 hours, which is 420 minutes, a day.
steps: Sustained daily rate: 4,700 / 10 = 470 packs a day. Lowest day: 430.
Sustained rate as a share of the best day: 470 / 560 = about 84%.
Production days needed: 5,100 / 470 = 10.85, so round up to 11 full days.
If the buyer allowed only 10 production days, the required rate would be 5,100 / 10 = 510 packs a day, a gap of 40 packs a day above her sustained rate.
Takt time for 11 days: 5,100 / 11 = about 464 packs a day; 420 minutes / 464 = about 0.9 minutes per pack.
blocks.result: Kemi needs 11 production days at her proven rate. She will plan with 470 a day, not 560, and add buffer days separately. Ten days would require 510 a day, which her records say she cannot hold.

blocks.text: Step 3: takt time, the order's heartbeat

**Takt time** is the available working time divided by the number of units the customer needs in that time. It tells you how often one finished unit must leave the line. In Kemi's case, one pack must come off the sealer about every 0.9 minutes. If any step takes longer than takt time per unit with its current people, that step needs help, a second machine or more hours. You will use takt time again in Module 3 to decide how many people each station needs.

blocks.title: Capacity is about good units
blocks.text: Only count units that pass your quality check. If 20 of 500 packs are underweight or burnt, your capacity that day was 480. Counting rejects as output hides the real rate and makes every later plan too optimistic.
Writing your capacity statement

Finish with one sentence you can say to any buyer: "With my current team and equipment I produce about 470 packs a day, so I can deliver 5,000 packs in 11 production days plus 4 days for checks, buffer and delivery." A statement like this, backed by your records, is far more convincing than "I can do it".

blocks.title: Do not buy capacity with unsafe speed
blocks.text: Pushing the bottleneck harder is where accidents happen. With hot oil, never overfill the pot (keep it no more than about one-third full), never leave it unattended, keep a fire blanket close, and never pour water on an oil fire. A burn or fire on day three destroys the whole plan.

takeaways: Time each step; the slowest step is the bottleneck and sets the pace.
Plan with your sustained daily rate from records, never your best day.
Takt time = available time divided by units required.
Count only good units as capacity.
Speeding up the bottleneck moves the bottleneck to the next slowest step.

activity.title: Measure your own capacity
steps: List every step of your process and who does it.
Time each step three times on a normal day and calculate units per hour.
Mark the bottleneck and the second slowest step.
Collect good-unit counts for 10 working days and calculate the average and lowest day.
Write your one-sentence capacity statement.
activity.evidence: Your timing table with the bottleneck circled, your 10-day output record and your capacity statement.

lessons.title: Material requirements for the whole run: bill of materials, allowances and purchase timing
objectives: Multiply a bill of materials by the planned quantity, with waste and overrun allowances
Subtract stock on hand and round up to the pack sizes suppliers sell
Set order dates from each supplier's lead time and the material's shelf life
Plan perishable materials in lots instead of one big purchase

blocks.text: Running out of one small item can stop a bulk run as surely as a broken machine. A missing roll of labels can leave 1,000 sealed packs that cannot be shipped. This lesson shows how to calculate everything the full order needs, buy it in the right amounts, and have it arrive in time without paying for stock that spoils.

blocks.name: package
blocks.caption: Pouches, labels and cartons are as critical as the main ingredient in a bulk run.

blocks.text: The bill of materials

A **bill of materials (BOM)** lists every material in one unit and how much of it. Build it from your own weighed batches, not from memory. Include packaging and the share of each carton. For a pack of chips the BOM includes raw plantain, oil, salt and seasoning, one printed pouch, one label and one fiftieth of a carton.
Three allowances to add

items: **Overrun:** extra units you plan to make so that quality samples and rejects do not leave you short. Kemi plans 2%, so 5,100 packs for an order of 5,000.
**Material waste:** loss before a unit exists, such as bruised plantain or trimming. Use your own records; Kemi adds 5% on plantain.
**Packaging spoilage:** pouches lost to bad seals or misprints. Kemi adds 3% on pouches and labels.

blocks.text: Next, subtract what is already in your store and check its condition. Then round up to how suppliers actually sell: pouches in packs of 500, labels in rolls, oil in 25-litre kegs. Finally, ask each supplier for their **lead time**, the days between paying and receiving the goods. Printed pouches with a buyer's logo often take longest because artwork must be approved first.

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi's material requirements for 5,100 packs
blocks.context: For example, Kemi's BOM per pack is 0.30 kg raw plantain, 0.025 litres oil, 1.5 g salt and seasoning, 1 pouch, 1 label and 1/50 carton. She has no printed pouches in stock and 3 empty cartons she will keep as spares.
steps: Plantain: 5,100 x 0.30 = 1,530 kg, plus 5% waste = 1,530 x 1.05 = 1,606.5 kg. She plans to buy about 1,607 kg.
Oil: 5,100 x 0.025 = 127.5 litres. In 25-litre kegs: 127.5 / 25 = 5.1, so she buys 6 kegs (150 litres).
Salt and seasoning: 5,100 x 1.5 g = 7,650 g, about 7.7 kg.
Pouches and labels: 5,100 x 1.03 = 5,253 each. Sold in packs of 500: 5,253 / 500 = 10.5, so she orders 11 packs = 5,500.
Cartons: 5,000 / 50 = 100 for delivery, plus 5 new spares = 105.
blocks.result: Kemi's purchase list: about 1,607 kg plantain, 6 kegs of oil, about 7.7 kg salt and seasoning, 5,500 pouches, 5,500 labels and 105 cartons. The rounded-up extras (247 pouches, 22.5 litres of oil) are a known cost she will include in her price.

blocks.text: Timing the purchases

Materials split into two kinds. **Long-lead, long-life** items such as printed pouches, labels and cartons should be ordered first, as soon as the deposit arrives and the artwork is approved. **Perishable** items, here plantain, must not all arrive on day one: 1.6 tonnes would ripen and soften before Kemi could fry it. She buys plantain in four lots of about 400 kg, each arriving the day before it is needed, and asks her market supplier to hold the same ripeness each time.

blocks.title: When each material is ordered
items: Deposit received: order pouches
Artwork approved: labels, cartons
Day before production: oil, plantain lot 1
Mid-run: plantain lots 2 to 4
Last day: count leftovers
blocks.caption: Long-lead items are ordered first; perishable materials arrive in lots just before they are needed.

head: Material
Lead time
Order by
rows: In four lots, each the day before use

blocks.title: Confirm specification on arrival
blocks.text: When each delivery arrives, check it against your specification before you sign or pay the balance: pouch size and print against the approved artwork, oil keg seals intact, plantain firmness and ripeness. A wrong print found on arrival costs a phone call; found after filling 2,000 pouches, it costs the order.

blocks.title: Store food materials safely
blocks.text: Keep oil and food materials off the floor on pallets or shelves, covered, away from chemicals, fuel and pests, and use the oldest stock first. Store pouches in their sealed cartons until use so the food-contact side stays clean.

Write all this into one **material requirements sheet**: material, quantity needed, stock on hand, quantity to buy after rounding, supplier, lead time, order date and arrival date. In the next module you will place these dates on the full production schedule.

takeaways: Build the bill of materials from weighed batches, including packaging.
Add overrun, material waste and packaging spoilage allowances.
Subtract stock, then round up to supplier pack sizes and include the extra in your cost.
Order long-lead items first and buy perishables in lots.
Check every delivery against specification before signing for it.

activity.title: Build your material requirements sheet
steps: Write the bill of materials for one unit of your product, weighing each input.
Multiply by your planned quantity and add your three allowances.
Subtract stock on hand and round up to supplier pack sizes.
Phone or message each supplier to confirm lead time and price, and set order dates.
activity.evidence: Your completed material requirements sheet with supplier names, lead times and order dates.

quiz.q: A buyer sends: "Need 3,000 bottles of liquid soap before month end, price?" What should you do first?
options: Quote your usual retail price minus 10%
Ask for quantity, specification, packaging, delivery details and payment terms, then send a written quote and sample
Start buying materials so you are ready
Decline, because the order is larger than normal
quiz.explain: A bulk enquiry rarely contains enough detail to price or plan. Turn it into a written specification sheet first.

quiz.q: Kemi's steps run at 120, 80, 150, 90 and 200 packs per hour. What is the most the line can produce in one hour?
quiz.explain: The line can never move faster than its slowest step, the bottleneck, which is frying at 80 packs an hour.

quiz.q: Your last 10 days produced 4,200 good units in total. Your best day was 520. An order needs 4,600 units. How many production days should you plan?
options: 11 days, using the sustained rate of 420 a day
quiz.explain: Sustained rate = 4,200 / 10 = 420. 4,600 / 420 = 10.95, so round up to 11 days. Planning from the best day would promise too early a finish.

quiz.q: You need 2,140 labels, and labels are sold in rolls of 500. How many rolls do you buy?
quiz.explain: 2,140 / 500 = 4.28, and you cannot buy part of a roll, so round up to 5 rolls (2,500 labels).

quiz.q: Why does Kemi buy 1.6 tonnes of plantain in four lots instead of all at once?
options: Suppliers never sell more than 400 kg
Buying in lots always gives a lower price
Plantain is perishable and would ripen and soften before she could fry it all
quiz.explain: Perishable materials should arrive just before they are needed so their quality matches the approved sample throughout the run.

quiz.q: An order is for 2,000 units and you plan a 3% overrun. How many units do you schedule?
quiz.explain: 2,000 x 1.03 = 2,060 units, so samples and rejects do not leave you short of the 2,000 promised.

modules.title: Scheduling, Quality Gates and the Money Plan
modules.overview: With the order sized, you now fix dates, protect quality across thousands of units and make sure you can afford the run before the buyer pays. You will build a backward schedule with milestones, design quality gates with a stop rule, and cost the order with a week-by-week cash plan and payment terms.

lessons.title: Backward scheduling: start date, milestones, buffers and the daily tracker
objectives: Work backwards from the delivery date to find the latest safe start date
Place milestones at 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of output
Build buffer days into the plan instead of planning to finish exactly on time
Track planned against actual output every day and act on a shortfall early

blocks.text: Most late deliveries are decided on the first day, when the producer starts too late. **Backward scheduling** fixes this. You start from the delivery date and subtract every stage, from the last to the first, until you reach the latest date you can safely begin. Then you place checkpoints along the way so a shortfall shows up while it is still small.

blocks.name: schedule
blocks.alt: A woman arranging tasks on a large calendar
blocks.caption: Working backwards from the delivery date shows the real start date, which is usually earlier than instinct suggests.

blocks.text: The stages, last to first

items: **Delivery:** the agreed date, including travel time to the buyer.
**Final check and loading:** count cartons, pre-shipment quality check, delivery documents.

**Buffer:** working days kept empty to absorb power cuts, sickness or a bad batch. Many planners hold back 10 to 20% of the production days; choose a figure that matches your own record of disruptions.
**Production:** planned units divided by your sustained daily rate, rounded up.
**First-article run:** a short run to confirm the line matches the golden sample before full speed.
**Materials in:** the latest arrival date for everything needed on day one, which in turn sets each order date from its lead time.

blocks.text: Count **working days**, not calendar days. Decide which days your workshop works (for example Monday to Saturday), and mark public holidays, market days when your supplier is closed, and any family or church commitments you cannot move. A plan that quietly counts Sundays will be two days late before it starts.

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi's backward schedule
blocks.context: For example, Kemi must deliver 5,000 packs on Thursday 10 December 2026. She works Monday to Saturday. Production is 11 days at 470 packs a day for 5,100 planned packs. She keeps 2 buffer days, 1 day for final check and loading, and 1 day for a first-article run. Printed pouches take 10 working days to arrive.
steps: Delivery: Thursday 10 December.
Final check and loading: Wednesday 9 December.
Buffer days: Monday 7 and Tuesday 8 December (Sunday 6 December is not a working day).
Production: 11 working days ending Saturday 5 December, so starting Tuesday 24 November.
First-article run: Monday 23 November.
All materials for day one in by Saturday 21 November. Counting back 10 working days, pouches must be ordered by Tuesday 10 November.
blocks.result: Kemi must confirm the order, receive the deposit and approve pouch artwork by Tuesday 10 November, a full month before delivery. Without the backward schedule she might have started thinking about it in late November.

blocks.text: Milestones and the daily tracker

Split output into checkpoints. For 5,100 packs, 25% is 1,275, 50% is 2,550, 75% is 3,825 and 100% is 5,100. At 470 a day, Kemi should pass 1,275 during day 3 (1,410 by its close), 2,550 during day 6 (2,820), 3,825 during day 9 (4,230) and finish on day 11. She writes these targets on a sheet on the wall, or in a shared Google Sheet, and fills in actual good packs each evening.

The **gap** column is the most important number in the run. In this example, Kemi is 70 packs behind after three days, about 5% of plan. That is easy to recover now: one extra hour at the fryer on two days gives 160 packs. If she ignores it, the same trend leaves her about 250 packs short by day 11, with only buffer days left to fix it.

blocks.title: Kemi's backward schedule
items: 10 Nov: order pouches
21 Nov: materials in
23 Nov: first-article run
24 Nov to 5 Dec: production
7 to 8 Dec: buffer
9 Dec: check, 10 Dec: deliver
blocks.caption: Each date is found by subtracting the stage after it, so the start date is set by the delivery date.

blocks.text: Rules for acting on a gap

items: **Gap under 5% of plan:** recover inside normal hours, for example by reducing changeover or idle time at the bottleneck.
**Gap of 5 to 10%:** add planned extra time at the bottleneck only, within safe working hours.
**Gap over 10%, or buffer half used:** call the buyer the same day with the facts and a revised plan, such as a partial delivery on the date and the rest two days later.

blocks.title: Use the buffer last
blocks.text: Treat buffer days as the buyer's protection, not spare production time. If you plan to use them from the start, you have no protection left when a real problem arrives.

blocks.title: Free tools that work on a phone
blocks.text: A paper chart on the wall works well for a team. If you want a digital copy, Google Sheets lets you share one tracker with your supervisor so both of you can see the gap each evening.

takeaways: Start from the delivery date and subtract each stage to find the latest start.
Count working days and mark days you cannot work.
Set 25, 50, 75 and 100% milestones and record actual output daily.
Act on small gaps early; tell the buyer early when the buffer is at risk.
Buffer days protect the delivery date; do not plan to use them.

activity.title: Build your backward schedule
steps: Choose a delivery date for your sample order from Lesson 1.
List your stages and the working days each needs, using your capacity from Module 1.
Count back on a calendar to find the start date and the latest order date for each material.
Draw a daily tracker with cumulative plan, actual and gap columns.
activity.evidence: A photo of your backward schedule and empty daily tracker with milestones marked.

lessons.title: Quality gates across a long run: first article, interval checks and the stop rule
objectives: Place five quality gates from material receipt to pre-shipment
Set an interval sampling plan with clear pass and fail measures
Apply a stop rule when a defect pattern appears
Calculate defect rates and keep a run quality log

blocks.text: On a small order you check each unit at the end. On a run of 5,000 you cannot, and a problem found at the end may already be inside thousands of units. The answer is **quality gates**: planned checkpoints throughout the run, each with a clear measure, a sample size and a rule for what happens on a fail.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: A simple check sheet at each gate catches a problem within a few hundred units, not a few thousand.

blocks.text: Five gates for a bulk run

blocks.title: Quality gates through the run
items: Gate 1: materials received
Gate 2: first article each day
Gate 3: interval checks
Gate 4: end-of-day count
Gate 5: pre-shipment check
blocks.caption: Each gate stops a different kind of problem before it travels further down the line.

items: **Gate 1, materials received:** check each delivery against specification (print, size, seals, freshness) before it enters the store.
**Gate 2, first article each day:** the first units of each day are compared side by side with the golden sample before full speed.
**Gate 3, interval checks:** a small sample is checked at a fixed interval, for example 5 packs every 100 packs.
**Gate 4, end-of-day count:** good units counted, rejects counted and recorded, cartons marked with the date or batch code.
**Gate 5, pre-shipment check:** a sample drawn from different cartons before loading.

blocks.text: Measures that anyone can apply

Each check must be something a trained worker can decide the same way every time. Write the measure and the limit. For Kemi's packs: **weight** on a digital scale, no pack under the 100 g stated on the label (she sets her filling target at 103 g so normal variation stays above 100 g); **seal** with no gaps when gently pulled; **colour** within the light and dark reference chips taped beside the station; **crunch and taste** on one chip per check.

blocks.title: Check your scale every morning
blocks.text: A scale that reads wrong ruins every weight check. Each morning, weigh an object of known weight, such as a sealed 1 kg pack of sugar from a reliable brand or a test weight, and write the reading in the log. If it is off, fix or replace the scale before filling.
The stop rule

Decide in advance what pattern stops the line. Kemi's rule: **if 2 or more of the 5 sampled packs fail any measure, stop that station**, find the cause, fix it, then check the last 100 packs one by one before restarting. Common causes in long runs are a worn sealer element, a new lot of material that behaves differently, oil that needs changing, or a tired worker late in the day. Each needs a different fix, so find the cause before restarting.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading day 4 of the quality log
blocks.context: For example, on day 4 Kemi's team made 480 packs and ran 5 interval checks of 5 packs each. Results: check 1, 0 fails; check 2, 0 fails; check 3, 1 underweight; check 4, 2 underweight; check 5 not yet done. The weigher has changed scoops after lunch.
steps: Packs sampled so far: 4 checks x 5 = 20 packs; fails = 0 + 0 + 1 + 2 = 3.
Sample fail rate: 3 / 20 = 15%, against near zero on days 1 to 3.
Check 4 has 2 fails, so the stop rule applies: sealing and filling stop.
Cause found: the new scoop holds less, so fills average about 99 g.
Fix: return to the marked scoop and re-weigh the last 100 packs one by one; 11 are under 100 g and are opened and refilled.
Log entry: date, time, check number, fails, cause, action, and who approved the restart.
blocks.result: The problem was contained to 100 packs, with 11 refilled, instead of being found at delivery inside thousands of packs. The log also shows the buyer, if asked, that her checks work.

blocks.text: Defect rate and rework allowance

At the end of each day calculate the **defect rate**: rejected units divided by units made. If Kemi rejects 9 of 480 packs, that is 9 / 480 = about 1.9%. Compare it with the 2% overrun she planned in Module 1. If the defect rate stays above the overrun, the plan will run short, so treat it like an output gap and act early.

blocks.title: When a buyer mentions AQL
blocks.text: Large buyers sometimes inspect the finished lot using acceptance sampling by attributes, published as ISO 2859-1, where an acceptance quality limit (AQL) and the lot size set how many units they sample and how many defects they accept. If a buyer names an AQL, ask for their sample size and accept and reject numbers in writing, and run your own Gate 5 the same way before they arrive.

blocks.title: Food hygiene does not slow down for deadlines
blocks.text: Follow the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food throughout the run: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials. Handwashing, hair covers and clean surfaces are never skipped to save time, and anyone with diarrhoea or vomiting stays away from food handling.

takeaways: Use five gates: materials, first article, interval checks, end of day, pre-shipment.
Write each measure and its limit so everyone judges the same way.
Set a stop rule in advance and find the cause before restarting.
Compare the daily defect rate with your planned overrun.
Keep a quality log; it is evidence for this buyer and the next.

activity.title: Design your quality gate plan
steps: Write the five gates for your product and what is checked at each.
Set measurable limits for two or three key qualities.
Choose your interval sample size and your stop rule.
Make a one-page quality log with columns for time, sample, fails, cause, action and sign-off.
activity.evidence: Your gate plan, stop rule and a blank quality log sheet, photographed.

lessons.title: Costing the run, the cash gap and payment terms that fund production
objectives: Build a full bulk cost including rounding, temporary labour, energy and contingency
Set a bulk price that keeps a healthy margin
Draw a week-by-week cash plan and find your lowest cash point
Negotiate deposit and balance terms that close the cash gap

blocks.text: A large order can make a business poorer if it is priced from small-batch costs or a quick discount. Bulk orders bring costs you do not see on a normal week: temporary workers and their training days, extra energy, the rounded-up packaging you must buy, delivery, and money tied up for weeks before the buyer pays. This lesson costs the whole run, then checks whether you can carry it until payment.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person working out figures with a large calculator
blocks.caption: Costing the whole run, not one unit, shows the real profit and the cash you need.

blocks.text: Cost the run from your purchase list

Use the quantities you will actually buy, after rounding, not the theoretical amounts. Then add labour for every person and every day, including training days, energy for each production day, delivery, the first-article trial and a **contingency**, a small reserve for surprises. Kemi uses 5% of her direct costs.

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi's full run cost and price
blocks.context: For example, using approximate Ibadan market prices Kemi gathered herself: plantain about N900 per kg, oil about N75,000 per 25-litre keg, pouches about N60 and labels about N25 each, cartons about N1,500. Labour: 3 regular workers at N6,000 a day for 11 days and 2 temporary workers at N5,000 a day for 13 days (11 plus 2 training days). Gas about N25,000 per production day. Delivery N60,000, trial N20,000.
steps: Materials: plantain 1,607 x 900 = N1,446,300; oil 6 x 75,000 = N450,000; salt and seasoning N40,000; pouches 5,500 x 60 = N330,000; labels 5,500 x 25 = N137,500; cartons 105 x 1,500 = N157,500. Total N2,561,300.
Contingency 5%: N162,215. Full run cost N3,406,515, or about N681 per pack delivered.
At a bulk price of N950 a pack: revenue 5,000 x 950 = N4,750,000; profit N1,343,485, about 28% of revenue.
blocks.result: Kemi's true cost is about N681 per pack, not the roughly N468 per pack that her bill of materials alone suggested (0.30 kg plantain N270, oil N75, seasoning about N8, pouch N60, label N25, carton share N30). N950 leaves a healthy margin. A price of N700, which might have looked generous for a big order, would have left almost nothing.

blocks.text: The cash gap

Profit is not cash. Kemi pays for pouches in early November, plantain and wages through late November, and the buyer pays the balance after delivery. List every payment out and in, by date, and keep a running balance. The lowest point is your **cash gap**: the money you must find from savings, a loan or better terms.

head: Date
Cash in or out (N)
Running balance (N)
rows: 21 to 23 Nov: oil, seasoning, plantain lot 1, trial
25 Nov to 2 Dec: plantain lots 2 to 4
28 Nov and 5 Dec: wages and gas

blocks.title: The bulk cash cycle
items: Deposit in
Buy packaging
Buy materials and pay wages
Deliver
Balance in
blocks.caption: Cash goes out for weeks before the balance comes in, so the lowest point in the cycle decides whether you can take the order.

blocks.text: With a 40% deposit Kemi must find about **N1,344,300** of her own money for over two weeks (the contingency is not counted here because it may not be spent). If she negotiates a 50% deposit (N2,375,000), the gap falls by N475,000 to N869,300. A third option is staged payment: for example 40% on order, 30% when the buyer approves the first-article packs, and 30% on delivery.
Payment terms to ask for

items: A deposit on order that covers at least the long-lead materials; 40 to 50% is a common request for large custom orders.
The balance on delivery, or within a short, written number of days, not "when we process it".
Payment to your business account by bank transfer or a payment link such as Paystack, with an invoice reference.
A written note that custom-printed packaging already bought is paid for even if the buyer cancels.

blocks.title: Check the money before you spend it
blocks.text: Only treat the deposit as received when it shows in your bank or wallet app balance. Fake transfer screenshots and SMS alerts are common. Do not order printed pouches on the strength of a promise or a purchase order alone.

blocks.title: The go or no-go line
blocks.text: Accept the order only if three things are true together: the schedule fits with buffer, the price leaves your target margin after contingency, and you can cover the cash gap without borrowing at a cost that eats the profit. If any one fails, negotiate the date, the price, the deposit or the quantity before you say yes.

takeaways: Cost the run from what you will actually buy, including rounding and training days.
Add a contingency and compare full cost per unit with your bulk price.
Profit is not cash: find your lowest cash point on a dated cash plan.
A bigger deposit or staged payments can close the cash gap.
Say yes only when schedule, margin and cash all work.

activity.title: Cost your sample order and find your cash gap
steps: Price every item on your material requirements sheet at current local prices, marked as approximate.
Add labour, energy, delivery, trial and a contingency to get the full run cost and cost per unit.
Choose a bulk price and calculate profit and margin.
List every payment in and out by date and find your lowest running balance.
Write the payment terms you would propose to close the gap.
activity.evidence: Your costing sheet, cash plan with the lowest point circled, and proposed payment terms.

quiz.q: Delivery is on a Friday. You need 1 day for final check, 2 buffer days and 6 production days, working Monday to Saturday. Final check is Thursday. Which day is the last production day?
quiz.explain: Counting back from Thursday: buffer days are Wednesday and Tuesday, so production must end on Monday of the same week.

quiz.q: After 4 days of a 10-day plan of 300 units a day, your cumulative actual is 1,050. What is the gap and what should you do?
options: Gap of 150 units, about 12.5%: tell the buyer today with a revised plan
Gap of 150 units: use the buffer days from now on
quiz.explain: Plan after 4 days is 1,200; 1,200 - 1,050 = 150, which is 12.5% of plan. Over 10% calls for early, honest contact with a revised plan.

quiz.q: At an interval check, 2 of 5 packs are underweight. Your stop rule says 2 fails stops the station. What comes next?
options: Carry on and check the next interval more carefully
Throw away the whole day's production
Stop, find the cause, fix it and recheck the last interval's units one by one before restarting
Add an extra scoop to every pack from now on without investigating
quiz.explain: The stop rule contains the problem. Finding the cause matters because different causes need different fixes.

quiz.q: You rejected 18 of 600 units today. Your plan had a 2% overrun. What does this tell you?
options: Defect rate 3%, above the overrun, so the order will run short unless you act
quiz.explain: 18 / 600 = 3%. If that continues, rejects will use up more than the 2% extra you planned to make.

quiz.q: Materials cost N2,000,000 and are paid before production. Wages and energy of N600,000 are paid during production. The buyer pays a 40% deposit of N1,400,000 and the balance after delivery. What is the cash gap before the balance arrives?
Which reason best explains why a bulk price must be calculated from the whole run, not by discounting your retail price?
options: Buyers always pay more for bulk
Bulk runs add costs such as temporary labour, training days, rounded-up packaging and contingency that a discount may not cover
It makes the quote look more professional
quiz.explain: Kemi's bill of materials alone suggested about N468 a pack, but the full run cost was about N681 once every bulk cost was included.

modules.title: People, Partners, Delivery and Your Bulk Readiness Plan
modules.overview: This module turns the plan into a working team and a finished delivery. You will compare ways to add capacity, including partner producers, staff the line using takt time, lead the run with daily huddles and safe hours, then deliver, review the run and package the evidence that wins the next bulk order.

lessons.title: When the order is bigger than you: extra hours, added stations, partner producers or split delivery
objectives: Calculate the extra daily output a larger order requires
Test four ways of adding capacity against the bottleneck, safety and quality
Set up a partner producer arrangement with one specification and one quality standard
Choose and present the option that protects the delivery date and your margin

blocks.text: Sometimes the order is larger than your sustained capacity can deliver by the date. You have four main levers: **work longer**, **add stations** (equipment and people), **share the work with a partner producer**, or **change the delivery** into parts. Each one changes cost, risk and quality differently, and only the numbers show which one works.

blocks.name: handshake-deal
blocks.alt: Two business people shaking hands on a deal
blocks.caption: A partner producer can add capacity, but only with one specification, one golden sample and clear terms.

blocks.text: Step 1: size the gap

Required daily output = planned units / production days available. Compare it with your sustained rate. The difference is the gap you must close. Remember the lesson from Module 1: when you speed up the bottleneck, the next slowest step takes over, so test each option against the whole line, not one step.

blocks.title: Worked example: the buyer asks for 8,000 packs by the same date
blocks.context: For example, a week after quoting, the HR officer asks Kemi whether she can supply 8,000 packs instead of 5,000 by 10 December. With a 2% overrun that is 8,160 packs in the same 11 production days. Her line runs 7 productive hours a day, and her sustained output is about 84% of the theoretical best.
steps: Required: 8,160 / 11 = about 742 packs a day, against her sustained 470. Gap: about 272 a day.

Option A, 2 extra fryer hours daily: best 80 x 9 = 720, sustained about 720 x 0.84 = 605. Still short, and 10-hour days for 6 days a week is 60 hours, above the 55-hour weekly level that WHO and ILO link to higher risk of stroke and heart disease. Rejected.
Option B, second fryer only: frying rises to 160 an hour, but sealing at 90 becomes the bottleneck. Best 90 x 7 = 630, sustained about 529. Far short.

Option C, second fryer, second sealer and a third peeler: peeling 180, frying 160, sealing 180, so seasoning at 150 becomes the bottleneck. Best 150 x 7 = 1,050, sustained about 881. Enough, but three new people to train and equipment to buy or hire within days.

Option D, partner producer: Kemi keeps her 5,100-pack plan. A trusted producer with a proven 300 packs a day makes 3,000 packs plus 2%, so 3,060 / 300 = 10.2, which is 11 days. Kemi supplies pouches and labels and inspects.
blocks.result: Option D closes the gap without changing Kemi's proven line, and Option C is the backup. Kemi offers the buyer 8,000 packs using a partner, or 5,000 on 10 December and 3,000 a week later if the buyer prefers her workshop alone to make everything.

blocks.title: Capacity options by gain and risk
items: Partner producer: big gain, managed risk
Added stations: big gain, high risk
Split delivery: no extra capacity, low risk
Longer hours: small gain, high risk
blocks.caption: The best option adds the most good units for the least new risk to quality, safety and the date.

blocks.text: Notice what the numbers show. Longer hours look free but add the fewest good packs and the most fatigue. Adding one machine alone barely helps, because the bottleneck simply moves. A split delivery adds no capacity at all, but it is often the safest answer when the buyer only needs part of the quantity on the first date, for example for an early event.
Making a partner arrangement work

Choose a partner whose work you have seen, not just heard about. Visit their workshop, watch a batch, and check their hygiene and their own records of daily output. Then put the arrangement in writing, even as a simple signed letter.

items: **Same specification:** the partner receives a copy of the order specification sheet and a golden sample.
**Controlled packaging:** you supply the printed pouches and labels and count them out, so the buyer's branding is only used for this order.
**Quantity, dates and milestones:** partner's daily target, and when you collect or receive each lot.
**Quality gates:** you or your supervisor check their first article and draw an interval sample from each lot; rejected packs are replaced at their cost.
**Price and payment:** price per accepted pack (for example N720), part paid on start and the rest on acceptance, so your margin is protected.
**Identification:** each carton marked with a partner code so any complaint can be traced.

blocks.text: On those example numbers, Kemi earns N950 - N720 = N230 per partner pack before her own costs of inspection and transport, which she estimates at about N20 a pack. That leaves about N210 a pack, or about N630,000 on 3,000 packs, less than on her own packs but with far less risk.

blocks.title: Be honest with the buyer
blocks.text: Some buyers require that they are told when part of an order is made by another producer. Tell the buyer about a partner in your quotation. You stay fully responsible for the quality and the delivery of every pack.

blocks.title: Build partners before you need them
blocks.text: The best time to find a partner producer is between bulk orders. Agree a trial order of a few hundred units, run your gates on it, and keep a short list of producers whose output and hygiene you have checked yourself.

takeaways: Size the gap first: required daily output minus sustained output.
Longer hours rarely close a large gap and raise health and quality risks.
Speeding up one station moves the bottleneck; test every option on the whole line.
A partner producer needs the same specification, golden sample, gates and written terms.
Offer the buyer options backed by numbers, including a split delivery.

activity.title: Test your capacity options
steps: Take your sample order and increase it by 60%.
Calculate the required daily output and the gap against your sustained rate.
Test longer hours, an added station and a partner producer against your whole line.
Draft the key terms of a partner arrangement on one page.
Write the message offering the buyer your recommended option.
activity.evidence: Your options calculation, draft partner terms and the message to the buyer.

lessons.title: Staffing and leading the run: line balancing, training temporary workers and safe hours
objectives: Use takt time to calculate how many people each station needs
Plan training and sign-off for temporary workers before production starts
Keep weekly hours within safe limits and plan rest
Run a kick-off briefing and a daily 10-minute huddle

blocks.text: A bulk run is won or lost by the team. Too few people at one station and the line waits; too many at another and you pay for idle hands. Untrained temporary workers can create more rework than output. Exhausted workers make mistakes and get hurt. This lesson shows how to size the crew, prepare new people and lead the run day by day.

blocks.name: team-work
blocks.alt: A team working together around a table
blocks.caption: Each person in the crew needs a clear station, a clear target and a clear quality rule.

blocks.text: Line balancing with takt time

For each station, measure the **work content**: the person-minutes needed to process a fixed number of units, such as 100. Divide it by the takt time for the same 100 units. The answer is how many people that station needs. Stations needing much less than one person can be combined, so one worker covers two light jobs.

blocks.title: Worked example: balancing Kemi's crew
blocks.context: For example, Kemi's target is 470 packs a day in 420 productive minutes, so takt time is 420 / 470 = about 0.89 minutes a pack, or about 89 minutes per 100 packs. From her timings in Module 1, the work content per 100 packs is: peel and slice 100 person-minutes, fry 75, season 40, fill and seal about 67, label and carton 30.
steps: Total work content: 100 + 75 + 40 + 67 + 30 = about 312 person-minutes per 100 packs.
Peel and slice: 100 / 89 = 1.1 people, so 2 people.
Fry: 75 / 89 = 0.8, so 1 person. Fill and seal: 67 / 89 = 0.75, so 1 person.
Season 40 / 89 = 0.45 and label 30 / 89 = 0.34. Combined 70 / 89 = 0.8, so 1 person can do both.
Crew: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5 people, with Kemi supervising and running quality checks.
blocks.result: Kemi moves from six people on five steps to a balanced crew of five. The two peeling places go to her two temporary workers after training, and the experienced staff keep the fryer, the sealer and seasoning with labelling.

blocks.title: Who does what in the run
items: Kemi: plan, buyer, sign-off
Supervisor: tracker and quality gates
Fryer and sealer: experienced staff
Peelers and packers: trained temporary staff
blocks.caption: Experienced people hold the bottleneck and quality-critical stations; temporary staff take the easiest stations to learn.

blocks.text: Check the balance on day one. If work piles up in front of one station while the next station waits, move a person or share a task until the flow is even. A small pile of work in front of the bottleneck is good, because the bottleneck should never stand idle; a growing pile anywhere else means that station is short of hands.
Training temporary workers

items: Hire early enough to train before production. Kemi budgets 2 paid training days, which is why her costing pays temps for 13 days, not 11.
Show, then do: the new worker watches a full cycle, then works beside an experienced person.
Teach the quality rule for their station using the golden sample, for example the slice thickness gauge.
Sign-off test: the worker produces a set amount, such as 30 plantains sliced, and passes three checks in a row before working alone.
Give hot-oil and knife safety rules on day one; temporary staff do not work the fryer.

blocks.title: Safe hours protect people and quality
blocks.text: A joint WHO and ILO study found that working 55 or more hours a week is linked to an estimated 35% higher risk of stroke and 17% higher risk of dying from ischaemic heart disease, compared with 35 to 40 hours. Kemi's plan of 8-hour shifts, 6 days a week, is 48 hours with one full rest day. Give regular breaks, water and a proper meal break, and rotate people on repetitive tasks.
The kick-off briefing

Before day one, gather the whole crew for 20 minutes. Explain the order size, the delivery date and why it matters; show the golden sample; give each person their station and daily target; explain the quality gates and the stop rule; and name the non-negotiables: hygiene, safety and no shortcuts on checks. Make it clear that anyone who sees a problem must speak up, and that stopping the line for a real defect is praised, not punished.
The daily 10-minute huddle

items: **Yesterday:** good units against plan, the gap, and the defect rate.
**Problems:** anything that slowed the line or failed a check, and what was done.
**Today:** target, any changes to stations, materials arriving.
**Thanks:** name one specific thing someone did well.

blocks.text: Keep the huddle short and standing, at the same time every morning, next to the tracker chart. When the run ends, pay everyone promptly and as agreed, thank the team specifically, and note which temporary workers you would call again.

blocks.title: Agree pay in writing
blocks.text: Give temporary workers a short written note of the daily rate, hours, training days and when they will be paid. Clear terms prevent disputes in the middle of a run.

takeaways: People per station = work content divided by takt time; combine light stations.
Put experienced staff on the bottleneck and quality-critical steps.
Train and sign off temporary workers before production starts.
Plan hours well below 55 a week, with a full rest day.
A clear kick-off and a daily 10-minute huddle keep everyone on plan.

activity.title: Plan your crew and huddle
steps: Work out takt time for your sample order and the work content per 100 units at each station.
Calculate people per station and draw your crew plan with names or roles.
Write a training and sign-off plan for one temporary worker.
Write your kick-off briefing as five bullet points and print a huddle sheet.
activity.evidence: Your line-balancing calculation, crew plan and kick-off briefing notes.

lessons.title: Delivery, run review and your bulk readiness portfolio
objectives: Prepare delivery documents and get signed proof of delivery
Run an after-action review comparing plan with actual results
Update your capacity statement from real run data
Assemble a bulk readiness portfolio and a 90-day plan

blocks.text: The order is not finished when the last pack is sealed. You still need a clean handover, payment of the balance, and a review that turns this run into better numbers for the next one. Done well, the records from one bulk order become the evidence that wins the next.

blocks.name: order-delivered
blocks.alt: A delivery being handed over at a door
blocks.caption: A counted, signed handover protects your payment and closes the order cleanly.

blocks.text: Delivery documents

items: **Invoice** with the order reference, quantity, unit price, deposit received and balance due, and your account details.
**Delivery note** listing the number of cartons, units per carton and total units, with any batch codes.
**Proof of delivery:** the receiver signs and dates your copy of the delivery note after counting, and writes their name. Take a photo of the signed note and the stacked cartons.
**Retained samples:** keep a few packs from each production day, labelled with the date, in case of a later quality question.

blocks.text: If the buyer agreed to a partial delivery, issue a delivery note for each part and show the running total delivered and outstanding. Count cartons together with the receiver before signing; a dispute about a missing carton is easy to settle at the door and very hard a week later. Send a WhatsApp message the same day with the photo of the signed note and a polite reminder of the balance due date.
The after-action review

Within a week, sit with your supervisor for 45 minutes and answer four questions: **What did we plan? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we do differently next time?** Use the tracker, the quality log and your cash records, not memory.

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi reviews the 5,000-pack run
blocks.context: For example, Kemi planned 5,100 packs in 11 production days. A power cut on one day cut output to 180 packs, so she used one of her two buffer days for production. Total made: 5,210 packs. Rejected: 98. She delivered 5,000 packs on 10 December.
steps: Good packs: 5,210 - 98 = 5,112. Defect rate: 98 / 5,210 = about 1.9%, inside the 2% overrun.
Production days used: 12. Average good packs a day: 5,112 / 12 = 426.
Without the power-cut day: (5,112 - 180) / 11 = about 448 a day, below the 470 she planned with.
Spare good packs: 5,112 - 5,000 = 112, sold through her normal retail customers.
Cause found for the lower rate: temporary peelers were slower in the first three days than in the sign-off test.
blocks.result: Kemi delivered on time because of the buffer, not because the plan was exact. Next time she will plan with about 450 packs a day, give temps one more training day, and arrange a backup generator or a fryer fuel that does not depend on grid power.

blocks.title: Each run improves the next
items: Plan with records
Run and track
Deliver and get paid
Review plan against actual
Update capacity and costs
blocks.caption: The after-action review feeds real numbers into the next quote, so every bulk order is planned better than the last.

blocks.text: Review the money as well as the output. Compare actual spending on each cost line with the costing sheet, check whether the contingency was used, and record when the balance actually arrived against the agreed date. These three figures improve your next price, your next contingency and the payment terms you ask for.
Your bulk readiness portfolio

Buyers who place big orders want proof that you can deliver. Keep a simple folder, printed and as a PDF on your phone, with: your **capacity statement** updated from real runs; a one-page summary of each completed bulk order (product, quantity, dates, on-time result, defect rate) with the buyer's permission to mention them; photos of your line, your quality log and your storage; and your standard bulk terms. If you have not yet completed a bulk order, include the capacity calculation, backward schedule and quality gate plan from this course as evidence that you plan properly.

blocks.title: Ask for a reference while the delivery is fresh
blocks.text: A week after delivery, when the balance is paid, ask the buyer for two or three sentences you may quote, or permission to give their contact to future buyers. Specific words such as "5,000 packs, on time, consistent quality" are worth more than general praise.
Your 90-day plan

items: **Next capacity target:** for example, from about 450 to 700 good packs a day.
**What must change:** the actual constraint from your review, such as a second fryer and sealer, a backup power source, or a cash reserve that covers the gap.
**Partners and suppliers:** one tested partner producer and two checked suppliers for your main material.
**Buyers to approach:** three named organisations that buy in volume, with the date you will contact each.

blocks.title: Keep records safely
blocks.text: Store invoices, delivery notes and quality logs for each order together, and back up phone photos to cloud storage. Do not share buyers' contact details or staff phone numbers in your portfolio without their permission.

takeaways: Count cartons with the receiver and get a signed, dated delivery note.
Review plan against actual within a week, using your records.
Update your capacity statement with real run data, not the plan.
Keep a bulk readiness portfolio with evidence a buyer can check.
Set a 90-day plan built on the constraint your review revealed.

activity.title: Run a review and build your portfolio
steps: Draft an invoice and a delivery note for your sample order.
Answer the four review questions for a recent order, or for your sample plan.
Write your updated capacity statement.
Put your capacity calculation, schedule, quality plan, cash plan and review into one folder.
Write your 90-day plan with a capacity target and three named actions.
activity.evidence: Your delivery documents, review notes, capacity statement and 90-day plan in one folder or PDF.

quiz.q: An order needs 6,300 units in 10 production days. Your sustained rate is 480 a day. What is the daily gap?
quiz.explain: Required = 6,300 / 10 = 630 a day. Gap = 630 - 480 = 150 units a day.

quiz.q: Kemi adds a second fryer, doubling frying to 160 packs an hour. Sealing runs at 90 an hour. What happens?
options: Peeling becomes the bottleneck at 120 an hour
Sealing becomes the bottleneck, so the line rises only to 90 an hour
quiz.explain: Once frying is faster than sealing, sealing at 90 an hour is the slowest step and sets the pace.

quiz.q: Takt time is 90 minutes per 100 units. A station has 135 person-minutes of work per 100 units. How many people does it need?
quiz.explain: 135 / 90 = 1.5 people, and you cannot staff half a person, so the station needs 2 people (or 1 person plus help from a light station).

quiz.q: To meet a deadline, a supervisor proposes 11-hour shifts six days a week for three weeks. What is the best response?
options: Accept, because it is only three weeks
Reject it: 66 hours a week is above the 55-hour level linked to serious health risk, and tired workers cause defects; look at a partner producer, added stations or a split delivery
Accept, but skip the quality checks to save time
quiz.explain: 11 x 6 = 66 hours. WHO and ILO link 55 or more hours a week to higher risk of stroke and heart disease, and fatigue raises defects.

quiz.q: At delivery, the receiver says one carton is missing after you have left. What would have prevented the dispute?
options: Counting cartons together with the receiver and getting a signed, dated delivery note with a photo
Asking the driver to remember the count
quiz.explain: A joint count and signed proof of delivery settle the quantity at the door.

quiz.q: A run made 4,100 units and 82 were rejected. What was the defect rate?

finalQuiz.q: Which item is missing from this order specification: product, quantity, packaging, delivery date and address, price?
options: Payment terms, quality standard (approved sample) and a named contact
The number of workers you employ
finalQuiz.explain: A complete specification sheet also fixes payment terms, the agreed quality standard and the people who confirm changes.

finalQuiz.q: Your steps run at 60, 45, 70 and 55 units per hour. Productive time is 6 hours a day. What is the theoretical best day?
finalQuiz.explain: The bottleneck is 45 units an hour, so 45 x 6 = 270 units is the theoretical best.

finalQuiz.q: Why should a producer plan with her 10-day average rather than her best day?
options: The average is always exactly 80% of the best day
Long runs include fatigue, delays and cleaning time, so the average is what she can actually sustain
finalQuiz.explain: The sustained rate reflects normal disruptions. Buffer days are added separately for unusual ones.

finalQuiz.q: Takt time for an order is 420 minutes divided by 350 units. What is it?
finalQuiz.explain: 420 / 350 = 1.2 minutes. One finished unit must leave the line about every 1.2 minutes.

finalQuiz.q: You need 96.4 litres of oil and it is sold in 25-litre kegs. How many kegs do you buy?
finalQuiz.explain: 96.4 / 25 = 3.86, so you round up to 4 kegs (100 litres) and include the extra in your cost.

finalQuiz.q: Which material should be ordered first once the deposit lands?
options: Long-lead items such as printed packaging
Fresh produce for the whole run
finalQuiz.explain: Printed packaging often has the longest lead time; perishables are bought in lots just before use.

finalQuiz.q: Delivery is Saturday. You need 1 day for final check and 2 buffer days, working Monday to Saturday. When does production end?
finalQuiz.explain: Final check is Friday and the buffer days are Thursday and Wednesday, so the last production day is Tuesday.

finalQuiz.q: After 3 days of a 300-a-day plan your cumulative actual is 870. What does the tracker tell you?
options: You are 130 behind and must call the buyer
You are 30 units behind, about 3%: recover within normal hours
Nothing until the end of the run
finalQuiz.explain: Plan is 900; 900 - 870 = 30, about 3.3% of plan, a small gap to fix early inside normal hours.

finalQuiz.q: At an interval check, 3 of 5 sampled units have weak seals. What should happen?
options: Stop the sealing station, find the cause, fix it and recheck the units made since the last good check
Increase the sample to 10 next time and keep going
Send all units to the buyer and let them decide
Ignore it if the deadline is close
finalQuiz.explain: The stop rule contains a defect pattern to a small number of units and fixes the cause before more are made.

finalQuiz.q: Your full run cost is N2,800,000 for 4,000 units. You price at N900 a unit. What is your profit and margin?
A buyer offers to pay 100% within 30 days after delivery, with no deposit. Your cash plan shows a gap of N1,500,000. What is the best response?
options: Propose a deposit or staged payments that cover materials, with the balance on delivery, and confirm in writing
Ask for a screenshot of their bank balance
finalQuiz.explain: Deposits and staged payments are a normal way to fund large custom orders and close the cash gap.

finalQuiz.q: A partner producer will make part of your order. Which arrangement best protects quality?
options: Let them use their own packaging and recipe
Check their units only at the buyer's premises
Pay in full before they start
Give them the specification and golden sample, supply the branded packaging, check their first article and sample each lot
finalQuiz.explain: One specification, one golden sample, controlled packaging and your own gates keep partner units identical to yours.

capstone.title: Bulk Production Readiness Plan
capstone.brief: Plan a realistic bulk order for a product you make, at least 50 times your usual order size, and submit one readiness pack: specification sheet, capacity calculation, material requirements, backward schedule with quality gates, full costing with a cash plan and payment terms, crew plan, and a 90-day bulk growth plan.
steps: Write the order specification sheet for your sample order, including a golden sample description.
Time your process, identify the bottleneck, calculate your sustained daily rate from 10 days of records and the order's takt time, and state your realistic maximum order size for the date.
Build the bill of materials and material requirements sheet with allowances, rounding, lead times and order dates.
Draw a backward schedule with milestones, buffer days and the five quality gates marked, plus your stop rule.
Cost the full run with contingency, set a bulk price, draw a dated cash plan, find the lowest cash point and write the payment terms you will propose.
Balance your crew with takt time, plan training for any temporary workers and keep weekly hours within safe limits.
Write your capacity statement and 90-day plan, and put everything into one folder or PDF.
evidence: A capacity calculation showing your realistic maximum bulk order size and timeline
A backwards-planned production schedule for a sample bulk order, with quality-gate checkpoints marked
A cash-flow and payment-terms plan for funding production before a bulk buyer pays
Material requirements sheet with supplier lead times
Crew plan and quality log template
